The Field Manual

Modeling systems — and the organizations that build them.

A guided ascent through the Zen Analytics Workbench: from your first node on the canvas to a full data-center twin and the value streams that run on it.

2 worlds — architecture & organization live cost · latency · capacity AI on any model, even local runs on your laptop
Your guide

I'm the Architecture Yeti — spirit of architectural purity. I dwell above the snow line, leave no footprints in your dependency graph, and vanish the instant a god-object appears. Climb with me. I'll point out the crevasses.

Complexity is simplicity, deferred.

Base Camp · 00

Two worlds, one workbench

The Workbench is a canvas where you drag things, wire them together, and watch the numbers move. What those "things" are depends on which world a workspace lives in — and every workspace is stamped as one kind or the other the moment you make it.

◇
Architecture

Distributed-system primitives — Postgres, Kafka, Elasticsearch, field devices, a whole data center — costed and latency-modeled as you build. Answers “will it scale, and what will it cost?”

◎
Organization

People, roles, meetings and documents; reporting lines and cross-functional flows. Answers “who does the work, how loaded are they, and where does the process stall?”

They aren't two apps bolted together — they're two ends of the same idea. Conway's Law says a system inevitably mirrors the communication structure of the org that ships it. Model the org and the architecture in the same tool and you can design both sides of that mirror on purpose.

The Yeti says

Team boundaries become service boundaries whether you plan them or not. You may as well plan them.

What you'll be able to do by the summit

Design an architecture from a sentence; find where it breaks first; lay it into racks with real power and cooling budgets; model the org that runs it; measure a value stream in cycle time and Six Sigma; publish it all as a service with a live cost; and export the whole thing to PDF, Word, or a wiki.

Camp One · 01

The lay of the land

Every workspace shares the same six regions. Learn them once and both worlds feel identical.

  1. Workspace switcher — top-left dropdown. Jump between workspaces, spin up a New workspace (architecture) or New organization, or load a bundled Sample architecture. An ORG badge marks organization workspaces.
  2. The two mode toggles — Architect / Analyze in an architecture space, Design / Analyze in an org. The left one is for building; the right flips the same canvas into read-only analysis.
  3. The ribbon — context tools for the current world: Compare, Scaling, Load, Firewall, Report, Catalog, Cards, Settings. It re-labels itself per world, so you never see architecture tools in an org.
  4. The palette — everything you can drag onto the canvas, searchable and filtered (All / Open-source / Azure / AWS in architecture; People / Meetings / Documents in an org).
  5. The inspector — select any node to edit its real config schema and see its live numbers. Empty until you pick something.
  6. The analysis strip — the bottom bar re-costs the whole model on every change. This is the number that matters, always in view.
The workload knobs

Just under the header sit the sliders that drive everything downstream — Records · Queries/day · Skew in architecture, Work items/mo · Hours/item in an org. Nudge them and the entire model re-sizes for the new load. Treat them as the “what-if” dial.

A system at rest reveals its shape.

Camp Two · 02

First ascent — model an IoT system

New workspace, hit Architect, describe it in a sentence: “an IoT seismic monitoring network — a fleet of ground-motion sensors streaming to a Kafka ingest, real-time event detection, raw waveforms to object storage, metrics to a TimescaleDB cluster, detected events in Elasticsearch, and a query-and-alert API.” Claude returns it wired and costed (that's Fig 01). We'll read that design, because it tells the whole story of how this tool thinks.

Reading a node

Every card shows its class (EDGE · SOURCE, AZURE · MESSAGING…) and its live vitals: p50 / p99 latency, throughput, storage, and $/mo. Connections carry a real wire protocol and port, assigned automatically per service. Select the sensor fleet and the inspector shows what a field device actually is.

The aggregate load — every source summed

Open Load in the ribbon and you don't get a per-device average — you get the aggregate: every sensor's rate summed across the fleet. That combined number, not the single-device rate, is what the ingest, the stream processor, and the time-series store all have to survive.

Aggregation is the whole point

A single sensor emits a handful of events a second. Five thousand of them is a different system. The Workbench propagates each fleet's load downstream — converging sources sum on the ingest, and the same aggregate lands on the stream processor and the stores. Every node is sized for the number it will actually see: the sum of everything upstream. Push the Records / Writes / Skew dials and watch it all re-size at once.

Building your own

  1. Drag from the palette — grab a store, a queue, a cache, a field device. Drop it on the canvas.
  2. Wire the ports — drag from a node's edge handle to another. The protocol and port attach themselves.
  3. Tune it — open the inspector, set the config, or hit Tune with expert to let a per-product domain expert (Elasticsearch, SQL Server, Redis…) recommend settings.
  4. Watch the strip — the bottom bar re-costs the whole system continuously. No “calculate” button; it's always live.

The four views

Logical

The design itself — nodes, flows, protocols. Where you spend most of your time.

Physical

Placement and security posture: on-prem vs edge zones, with cross-zone links flagged where a firewall would block them.

Network

Data-center / domain boxes with ports and per-link bandwidth. Movable, resizable.

Racks

The physical twin — real machines in real racks. Its own camp, just ahead.

Analyze — “where will it break first?”

Flip to Analyze and the bottom strip gains tabs: Bottlenecks, Costs, Network, Events, Capacity. The Scaling view is the one to memorize — it ranks every node by its binding constraint (compute, disk IOPS, memory, cluster nodes) and tells you how much headroom remains before growth saturates it.

Claude drew the first pass — and rewrites it in place

That whole seismic system came from one sentence to Architect. Already have a design? The same panel modifies it in place: “add a Redis cache in front of the query API,” or “give the TimescaleDB cluster three more nodes.” It edits the live spec rather than starting over.

Camp Three · 03

The physical plane — racks & power

Switch to the Racks view and the design stops being an abstraction. Now it's steel: named servers in numbered racks, in a named hall, in a real location — with power, heat, weight and money to account for.

racks · 79 mach.

Everything is derived, not typed in: heat follows load, energy follows PUE, weight rolls up per square metre, capex sums the bill of materials. Drag a server into a rack and every one of those figures moves. Feeds are modeled 2N so you can see what survives a utility failure — and you can even ask AI to design a rack for you.

From logical to physical, automatically

You rarely place 79 machines by hand. Size the logical design first; the Workbench proposes the hardware and racks to carry it, then you refine. The sub-views — Rack elevation · Data-centre floor · Cabling · Azure — are the same twin seen four ways.

From on-prem racks to Azure, with a prompt

That last sub-view is where the physical build-out becomes a cloud one. Switch to the Azure tab and hit Design Azure with AI: it takes your racked data-centre as context and translates each tier to its Azure equivalent — the right VM family and size per tier, managed disks snapped to real SKU boundaries, an ExpressRoute circuit back to whatever stays on-prem, and a container registry — reserving the steady-state capacity and costing it against live Azure pricing. A prompt steers it (“keep the ingest pay-as-you-go, reserve the TimescaleDB.”) The on-prem design is the question; Azure is the answer, and you can read the before/after side by side.

Design the calm, and the scale will follow.

Camp Four · 04

The other summit — model an organization

Open the switcher and choose New organization. The palette becomes people. Now you're modeling the other half of Conway's mirror: roles, meetings, documents, and the reporting lines between them.

The capacity ledger

This is the heart of org mode. Roles supply hours; meetings consume them. From that the Workbench derives:

60 FTE
Headcount
$1.5M
/mo · people + process
18%
Coordination tax
49 FTE
Effective heads
2.4
Span of control

Coordination tax is the share of capacity eaten by ceremonies — here 18%, so of 60 people only about 49 are effectively left to do the work. Push the demand knobs (work items/mo × hours/item) and utilization goes live on top of that effective capacity — with headroom when you're under and a growing-queue warning when you're over.

The Yeti says

Adding people to a late project makes it later — every new hire adds n communication paths. Watch span of control climb and remember Brooks.

Disconnected teams

If a cluster of roles has no reporting line home, the strip flags “disconnected teams — reconcile.” It's not an error; it's the model telling you an org island exists. Reconcile it, or decide it's intentional.

What an hour costs — the rate card

Every role carries a loaded $/hr, and the Rates ribbon opens the master table that sets it. Edit a rate once and it reprices every matching role on the canvas — and every new hire of that type. For government work, it also prices against the GSA schedule.

That one number is the foundation of the whole cost model: a role's monthly cost is FTE × loaded $/hr × hours/week × 4.33. Change the table and the capacity ledger, every swimlane's cost, and every service in the catalog all reprice at once.

Meetings — the coordination tax, itemized

A meeting node costs attendees × duration × times-per-month × rate on its own. But the tax — the capacity it actually eats — only lands when you say who attends: wire role → meeting (either direction) and each attendee is charged that ceremony's hours, scaled by the role's headcount.

Wire the attendees, or the tax reads zero

A ceremony wired to nobody still appears in the meeting total, but it's charged to no one — so coordination tax can read 0% even beside a full calendar. That gap between a meeting's declared attendee count and who's actually connected is deliberate: wire the roles and watch the tax land where it belongs.

Artifacts — documents, and who owns them

A document — an ADR, a runbook, a solution design — costs updates/mo × hours/update × author $/hr to keep alive; artifacts aren't free once written. Wire role → document to record who owns or authors it, and the inspector names the accountable owner by climbing the reporting chain. Steps can also produce artifacts: a generated playbook (next camp) drops its outputs onto the canvas as documents, each wired from the step that delivers it.

Camp Five · 05

Value streams — flow & Six Sigma

An org chart says who reports to whom. A value stream says how work actually flows across them. Add process-step nodes, wire role → step to drop a step into that role's lane and step → step to sequence the flow, then flip to Swimlanes.

5.5d
cycle time
8%
flow efficiency
3
handoffs
39%
rolled yield
1.2σ
sigma level

Read that strip like a diagnosis. Flow efficiency is work-time ÷ total time — 8% means the item spends 92% of its life waiting. Rolled yield compounds first-pass quality across steps; 39% means most of the effort is rework. Sigma level converts that yield to a Six Sigma score with DPMO, and even names the worst offending step.

This is your DMAIC surface

Cross-lane handoffs are where cycle time goes to die. The map shows you exactly which ones cross a lane and which step drags the sigma down — that's your Define/Measure done for you. Improve, then watch the numbers move.

Playbooks — make a step runnable

A swimlane tells you a step exists. A playbook tells someone how to actually run it. Select any process step, hit Generate playbook in the inspector (add a line of context if you like — “regulated change, needs security sign-off”), and a process-operations expert writes the operating guide for that one step:

Purpose & definition of done

Why the step exists and exactly what “finished” means.

Entry & exit gates

The criteria to start, and the criteria to hand off cleanly.

Task checklist & RACI

The ordered steps to do it, and who is Responsible / Accountable / Consulted / Informed.

Artifacts, tools & risks

What it needs, what it produces, and the risks with their controls.

The playbook is stored on the step as markdown and exports to PDF, Word, or the clipboard — so a modeled process becomes a runnable, shareable operating procedure. Every artifact it names is dropped onto the canvas as a document, wired from the step that produces it, so the process and its paperwork stay connected.

The Yeti says

A process you can't hand to someone else isn't a process — it's a habit. Write the playbook.

Latency is the space between intention and result.

Camp Six · 06

The service catalog

A service is a business capability — a process (the org workspace) plus the people, artifacts and software behind it. The catalog is where those get published, rolled up, and compared as one thing.

Services share people — so utilization is a portfolio

Here's the idea that ties it together. A service doesn't own a team; it draws on the org's shared people, and it's costed by effort (hours × rate × how often it runs) — not by burdening a whole salary. Add more services and each person's load accumulates across all of them. People Load shows that portfolio view: everyone's real utilization, once every service they touch is counted.

The Yeti says

One service looks cheap. Ten services sharing the same overworked staff engineer is a bottleneck with a name. Count the effort, not the headcount.

Camp Seven · 07

Reporting & sharing

A model nobody reads changes nothing. The Workbench turns any workspace into a shareable artifact — and lets you set two designs side by side before you commit.

Report

A full write-up — architecture, events, costs, scaling, resilience — to PDF, SVG, PNG, Markdown (wiki), Word or PowerPoint.

Compare

Two workspaces head-to-head on cost, latency, storage and resilience. The monolith-vs-split decision, quantified.

Firewall export

An AERB port-request (CSV / Markdown) of every cross-zone flow, generated from the network you drew.

Cards

Shareable summary cards of the model for a deck or a doc, without exporting the whole report.

Camp Eight · 08

The AI layer

AI runs through the whole Workbench — architecting designs, analyzing systems, tuning nodes with domain experts, generating inner-canvas logic — and it is provider-agnostic.

Any model

Anthropic Claude, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Point it at the model your team already uses.

Local & private

Run entirely offline against LM Studio, Ollama or vLLM on your own GPU. Real agentic tool-use works even on a local model.

Experts

Per-product tuners (Elasticsearch, SQL Server, Redis…) that recommend real config, not generic advice.

Keys stay home

API keys live server-side in .env and never reach the browser bundle. Your machine, your secrets.

No key? No problem.

Every AI panel has a fallback: run /architect "…" in Claude Code, paste or Load generated the spec, and you get the same result with no backend at all.

Between the nodes, the network.

The Summit · ▲

Zen Mode & the Yeti

You've reached the snow line. Press Ctrl + K and open Zen Mode — a calm space where computer-science lore drifts above a Himalayan temple: gradient descent, recursion trees, a breathing orb, slowly rotating koans, and the elusive Architecture Yeti.

Click any drifting law to learn it — Little's Law, the CAP theorem, the Universal Scalability Law, Euler's identity. Click the Yeti and it tells you its one rule: purity ≡ 1. It's a reward, a screensaver, and a quiet reminder of why we keep the layers clean.

The Yeti's rule

Sightings correlate with well-bounded contexts, honest interfaces, and a p99 that never spikes. Keep your layers pure — and I may bless your build.

Appendix · §

How the models work

Every number in the Workbench is produced by an explicit model — never a vibe. This appendix opens each one up: what real-world behaviour it simulates, the actual formula, the assumptions baked in, and the dials you turn to change it. The models are deliberately transparent and heuristic — built for relative comparison and “what-if,” and honest about being directional rather than a vendor benchmark.

One honest caveat up front

Two capacity engines live in the codebase: the shipping per-service models (hand-tuned per-unit constants; latency roughly flat in load) and a newer, physics-grounded M/M/1 queueing engine (latency explodes near saturation) that services opt into. Where they disagree, the queueing engine is the more realistic — and reconciling the two is an open design decision. The reference figures on each node card come from a lookup of published vendor/benchmark numbers, so the invented constants always sit next to grounded reality.

§1 Capacity · scaling · resilience · load

The chain from “a fleet emits load” to “which node breaks first, and when.” Load is offered by sources, propagated downstream, compared against three physical ceilings, and projected forward under growth.

Offered load — the device model

catalog/devices.ts
Simulates

What a fleet of field devices actually puts on the wire — events/sec, peak/sec, bytes/event, GB/day — in three emission styles.

The math

// discrete (LPR, GPS, sensors) — has a real avg↔peak gap readsSec = fleet × perDeviceDaily / 86400 readsPeak = fleet × peakPerMinute / 60 alertsSec = readsSec × alertRatePct/100 // stream (CCTV): eventsSec = fleet × fps; peak = avg (flat) // waveform (seismic): eventsSec = fleet × sampleRate × channels; peak = avg (flat) gbDay = avgBytesSec × 86400 / 1e9

Assumes

Discrete devices carry a genuine peak; stream and waveform sources set peak = average — which is exactly why CCTV and seismic read “flat” downstream while an LPR commuter fleet is spiky.

Dials
  • fleetCount / perDeviceDaily ↑ raises the mean (and everything downstream)
  • peakPerMinute ↑ widens the avg-to-peak gap (discrete only)
  • channels · sampleRate · bytesPerSample ↑ raises a seismic fleet's steady rate

“Where will it break first” — the binding constraint

analysis/capacity.ts · breakpoints.ts
Simulates

Every engine has three independent ceilings — compute (parallelism), disk I/O, and memory fit. The smallest one binds; a chain is only as strong as its weakest link. Offered load ÷ that ceiling is the utilisation you see.

The math

// compute ceiling — linear in the scaling knob, per category messaging: partitions × 15000 storage: vcores × 2500 × nodes search: min(shards×2500, dataNodes×4000) cache: memoryGb × 25000 × nodes // disk ceiling diskQps = IOPS / iosPerQuery, iosPerQuery = max(0.25, factor×3×(0.3 + miss×0.7)) // memory fit — working set spilling RAM derates compute linearly workingSet = recordCount × 256 × hot / 1e9, hot = clamp(0.05+(1−skew)×0.35, .05, .5) if workingSet > RAM: ceiling = compute × (RAM / workingSet) // binding = min(compute, disk, memory); a measured value overrides all

Projection

// month it saturates under monthly growth m = 1 + growth%/100 k = ln(capacity / offered) / ln(m) // null if k > horizon; 0 if already over cumulativeStorage += gbDay × 30 × (m^horizon − 1)/(m − 1) // geometric

Assumes

Ceilings are linear in the knob with hand-tuned per-unit constants. Load propagates as a superset union — a node behind two sources sees the sum of both means, with no fan-out splitting, sampling, or filtering. This model compares throughput only; latency lives in the queueing engine below.

Dials
  • the scaling knob (vcores, shards, nodes, partitions, memoryGb) ↑ raises the compute ceiling
  • cacheHitRatio ↑ → fewer disk I/Os → higher disk ceiling
  • recordCount ↑ grows the working set → memory binds sooner; skew ↑ shrinks the hot set → memory binds later
  • growth% · horizon ↑ pull the saturation month sooner

Latency under load — the queueing engine

analysis/resourceModel.ts
Simulates

The non-linear “cliff”: a design that's fine at average load falls over at peak. Standard operational-analysis / M/M/1 queueing, so response time climbs steeply as any resource approaches full utilisation.

The math

ρ = λ · D // utilisation = arrival rate × service demand R = D / (1 − ρ) // residence time per resource — blows up as ρ→1 response = Σ R + fixed_overhead p99 = mean × ln(100) ≈ 4.6× mean cacheHit = 1 − e^(−2 × cacheGb/workingSetGb) // saturating: ~86% at 1×, ~98% at 3×

Assumes

Single-server M/M/1 per resource (Poisson arrivals). ρ is capped at 0.995 so an overloaded queue returns a large finite latency plus an overloaded flag, not infinity. Three resources only (CPU / disk / net); no lock contention or GC. Fixed round-trip overhead is added to latency but excluded from utilisation — so a Redis GET floors at ~0.1 ms however fast the server.

Dials
  • arrival rate (λ) ↑ → ρ→1 → residence time explodes
  • memoryGb ↑ → higher hit ratio → fewer physical I/Os → lower disk ρ
  • disk tier / cores / netGbps ↑ → lower service demand on that resource

Resilience — RPO / RTO / blast radius

analysis/resilience.ts
Simulates

Disaster-recovery posture per node: RPO (worst-case data-loss window), RTO (time to restore service), and a size-based rebuild time. The system rolls up to the worst node on each axis.

The math

redundant = copies ≥ 2 (from replicationFactor / replicas) RPO: sync 0 · async 15s in-region / 60s cross-region · else backup interval · else ∞ RTO: stateless 45s · redundant 45s (auto) / 900s (manual) · backup → restore time · else ∞ blast radius = 600s provision + storageGb × 1000 / 200 MB/s // size-based rebuild object stores short-circuit: RPO 0, RTO 45s (multi-AZ, ~11 nines)

Assumes

Flat 200 MB/s restore and 600 s provisioning regardless of engine; constant replication lag; the rollup is a pure max — no correlated failures, split-brain, or dependency chains.

Dials
  • replicationFactor ≥ 2 → redundant → far lower RTO and RPO
  • dr.replicationMode (sync → RPO 0) · dr.multiRegion (flat 120 s failover) · dr.failover (auto 45 s vs manual 900 s)

Load propagation — size for the peak

analysis/diurnal.ts
Simulates

A fleet doesn't emit constant load — it follows a 24-hour curve (commuter AM/PM peaks, business hours, or flat). Converging fleets sum point-by-point and the aggregate flows downstream, so every node sees the actual time-varying load reaching it.

The math

// commuter: twin Gaussians at 08:00 & 17:36 on a 6% overnight floor level(h) = 0.06 + 0.94 × max( gauss(h,8,1.15), gauss(h,17.6,1.5) ) // affine fit so the curve's mean = daily total AND its max = target peak rate(t) = a + b·s(t), a = (avg − peak·sBar)/(1 − sBar), b = peak − a // converging sources add their 96-point vectors — staggered peaks only stack where they overlap

Assumes

Instant, lossless propagation — no transit delay, batching, or backpressure; the same rate vector is added unchanged to every downstream node (no fan-out division, no filtering/dedup). Fixed 15-minute resolution; all commuter fleets peak at exactly the same instants, so their peaks stack fully. Note the deliberate tension: the capacity model sizes on the mean, while this view exists to remind you to size for the peak.

Dials
  • diurnalProfile selects the shape (commuter / business / evening / flat / custom hand-plotted points)
  • peakPerMinute ↑ spikier curve; graph topology — more converging sources → higher summed peaks

Sizing — the reverse solver

analysis/sizing.ts
Simulates

The capacity model run backwards: from a plain-language target (QPS, users, ingest, dataset size, p95 SLA) solve for cluster shape — nodes, shards, replicas, provisioned RU/s, brokers — plus a monthly cost, and drop it straight onto the canvas.

The math

// tighter SLA → lower per-node utilisation target → more nodes for headroom utilFactor: 0.80 (≥200ms) → 0.62 → 0.48 → 0.34 → 0.25 (<20ms) search nodes = max(2, qps/(3000·util), users/(300·util)); shards = max(dataGb/40, ingest/12000) postgres vcores = clamp(qps/(1200·util), 2, 96); kafka partitions = max(3, ingest/10000)

Assumes

Fixed per-unit throughputs (3000 qps/node search, 1200 qps/vcore Postgres, 10k/partition Kafka), fixed shard-size targets and replication factors, fixed ~7× time-series compression. Explicitly “heuristic, for relative sizing.”

Dials
  • slaP95Ms ↓ (tighter) → more nodes via utilFactor
  • qps · ingest · concurrentUsers · dataGb each drive their own max() term
§2 Architecture — per-service cost & performance

Each service card's p50/p99, throughput, storage and $/mo come from a small explicit model. They share three foundations, then each service adds its own physics.

Shared foundations

catalog/nodeCatalog.ts · types
The rules
  • Every record = 256 bytes. The single biggest simplification — one constant (AVG_RECORD_BYTES) sizes every payload. (A schema type exists to derive real bytes later; no model uses it yet.) A few models override: Neo4j uses 64 B/node + 48 B/rel, Pinecone dim×4, Windows 512 B/op.
  • Rates: read QPS = queriesPerDay / 86400; write QPS = writePerDay / 86400.
  • Rounding hides infinity: the shared round() returns 0 for any non-finite value, so an ∞/NaN silently becomes 0.
  • Health: p99 > 800 ms → bottleneck, > 250 ms → warning. Several models tune their tails to cross these on purpose.
  • The saturation signature: most compute/messaging models compute sat = min(demand/ceiling, ~1.2) and add a quadratic sat² term to p99 — the fingerprint of a queue collapsing near capacity. The 1.2 cap means no model ever renders a fully-melted system.

PostgreSQL — cache-governed reads

nodeCatalog.ts:31
Simulates

A relational cluster where read latency is set by the buffer-cache hit ratio (cached ~1 ms, disk ~12 ms); the tail is inflated by misses and hot-row skew; indexes bloat storage.

The math

storage = recordCount × 256 × (1 + indexes×0.12) × replicas / 1e9 p50 = 1 + (1−hit)×12 p99 = p50 + (1−hit)×60 + skew×40 cost = storage×0.12 + nodes×vcores×45 + (indexes>12 ? 60 : 0)

Assumes

The write path isn't modelled at all (writePerDay ignored); connectionPool is a dial the math never reads; no throughput ceiling — QPS is pass-through.

Dials
  • cacheHitRatio ↑ lowers both p50 and p99 · indexes / replicationFactor ↑ storage · skew ↑ tail · nodes·vcores = cost only

Apache Kafka — partition-bound streaming

nodeCatalog.ts:80
Simulates

Throughput bounded by partitions × 12,000 msg/s; as write load nears that ceiling, consumer lag spikes as a quadratic. Compression × retention × replication set storage.

The math

ratio = {none:1, gzip:.35, snappy:.55, lz4:.5, zstd:.3} storage = writeQps × 256 × ratio × retentionH×3600 × rf / 1e9 sat = min(writeQps / (partitions×12000), 1.2) p50 = 3 + sat×20 p99 = p50 + sat²×200 // lag spike cost = storage×0.10 + brokers×220

Assumes

Reads/consumers ignored (queriesPerDay unused); flat 12k/partition regardless of message size; static compression ratios.

Dials
  • partitions ↑ raises the ceiling → eases the tail · retentionHours / rf ↑ storage · compression (zstd) ↓ storage · brokers = cost only

Elasticsearch — scatter-gather + GC

nodeCatalog.ts:194
Simulates

A query fans out to every shard; the coordination tail grows with log₂(shards). Both very large and very small JVM heaps hurt (GC) — a non-monotone penalty with a 8–32 GB sweet spot.

The math

scatter = log2(shards+1) × 12 gc = heap>32 ? 40 : heap<8 ? 25 : 8 // U-shaped p99 = 6 + scatter + gc + skew×30 storage = recordCount × 256 × 1.3 × (1+replicas) / 1e9

Assumes

Every query hits all shards (no routing); GC is a 3-bucket step; refreshIntervalS is inert; more shards genuinely hurt latency here.

Dials
  • shards ↑ widen the tail (real trade-off) · heapGb U-shaped via GC · replicas ↑ storage · dataNodes = cost only

Redis — memory-pressure cache

nodeCatalog.ts:139
Simulates

A 5% hot set (amplified by skew) must fit cluster RAM. When it overflows (pressure>1), the effective hit ratio degrades and the tail grows — eviction thrash.

The math

hotSet = recordCount × 256 × 0.05 × (1+skew) / 1e9 pressure = min(hotSet / (memGb×nodes), 3) effHit = pressure>1 ? hit/pressure : hit p50 = 0.4 + (1−effHit)×8 p99 = p50 + (pressure>1 ? pressure×6 : 1)

Assumes

Hot fraction hardcoded 5%; evictionPolicy is inert (LRU vs LFU = no effect); writes ignored.

Dials
  • memoryGb · nodes ↑ relieve pressure → lower latency · recordCount / skew ↑ grow the hot set

Join strategy — the complexity core

nodeCatalog.ts:246
Simulates

Joining a big left set against a smaller right one. Algorithm class (nested-loop quadratic / hash linear / sort-merge n·log n) × movement (co-located free / broadcast / shuffle) — with a skew tax and a straggler penalty on shuffle.

The math

nested = left × min(right,1e6) × 1e-9 hash = (left+right)×1e-7 shuffle bytes = (left+right)×256 skewTax = shuffle ? 1+skew×1.5 : 1+skew×0.3 p99 = p50×(1.4+skew) + (shuffle ? 200 : 0) // straggler

Assumes

The 1e-9/1e-7/1e-8 constants are calibration, not hardware; bandwidth fixed 1.25 GB/s; nested-loop right side capped at 1M so even the "catastrophic" case stays finite.

Dials
  • joinType picks the complexity class · strategy sets movement + skew sensitivity + straggler · parallelism ↓ CPU but ↑ broadcast bytes

Stream processor · TimescaleDB — windowing & retention

nodeCatalog.ts:388 · 499
Stream

cpuFactor = {tumbling:1, hopping:2.2, sliding:4} ceiling = units×20000 / cpuFactor p50 = watermarkS×1000×0.5 + sat×40 p99 = watermarkS×1000 + sat²×300

Latency is dominated by the watermark grace period (results emit at window close); sliding windows re-evaluate on every event (4× CPU) and keep 2× state.

Timescale

kept = min(retentionDays / timeSpanDays, 1) // the ONE model that reads timeSpanDays storage = recordCount × kept × 256 × (compressed ? 0.14 : 1) / 1e9 p99 = p50 + (compressed ? 35 : 8) + skew×20 // compression adds a cold-read tail

Compression is a genuine trade-off: ~7× smaller, but +35 ms decompressing cold chunks.

The breadth factories & sources

catalog/services.ts · devices.ts · windows.ts
Simulates

Beyond the hero engines, archetype factories stamp out the AWS/Azure/OSS catalog with per-service constants, all on the same 256-byte assumption:

Patterns
  • relational / nosql / queue / cacheSvc / warehouse / serverless / gateway / f5 — each a saturation model (sat² tail). nosql is the only one folding in both reads and writes (writes count 5×). warehouse carries high 200/400 ms floors (OLAP is slow).
  • objectStore — tier latency cliffs: hot 18 ms, cool 45 ms, archive 60,000 ms (rehydrate).
  • Field devices (deviceLoad) are sources, not consumers — they produce offered load; storage_gb reports GB/day generated, not accumulated. Devices, Windows services and workflow() ignore the Workload entirely, driving off their own config.
  • Windows / IIS — a thread-pool model: qps = concurrency × 1000/durationMs (Little's Law), plus a per-instance Windows Server license.
Inert dials

A handful of dials appear in the inspector but the math never reads them — modelled qualitatively, not quantitatively: Postgres connectionPool, Redis evictionPolicy, Elasticsearch refreshIntervalS, Timescale chunkIntervalDays, Pinecone metric, warehouse concurrency, F5 vips/persistence, Windows role.

§3 Physical plane & cloud pricing

The data-centre twin turns watts into heat, weight and money and checks it survives a feed failure; the cloud model translates the same design to Azure at live prices. Every ceiling is a Budget — amber at 75%, red at 90%.

Power — draw, derate & 2N failover

analysis/rackPower.ts · facility.ts
Simulates

Server draw rolling up to rack kW to facility kW, and the essential 2N check: can each redundant feed carry the whole rack when its partner dies?

The math

watts = idleW + (maxW − idleW) × util/100 // util defaults 50%, or the hosted node's live util circuitKw = amps × volts × (three-phase ? √3 : 1) × 0.8 / 1000 // 0.8 = NEC continuous-load derate requiredPerFeed = redundant ? drawKw : drawKw/feeds // 2N: one feed carries ALL totalKw = itKw × PUE energy$/mo = totalKw × 730 × $perKwh

Assumes

Draw is a linear idle→max interpolation (real curves are convex); a rack at 60% on both feeds is a failure, not a pass. PUE inflates the utility/generator/energy checks but not UPS/cooling (those are sized to IT load).

Dials
  • node utilizationPct ↑ → watts → the whole bill · PUE ↑ total kW & energy$ · rack.redundancy (2N/N+1) doubles required-per-feed · PDU amps/volts/phase = capacity

Heat · weight · floor loading

analysis/rackPower.ts · rackSpace.ts · facility.ts
The math

BTU/h = kW × 3412.14 tons = kW × 0.2843 // heat keyed to IT kW (heat to reject) peakFloorLoad = max over racks of (weightKg / footprintM²) // worst point-load, not room average roomArea = Σ footprint × 2.5 // AISLE_FACTOR: hot/cold aisles + clearance

Assumes

1:1 electrical→heat (true to first order); floor loading uses the bare enclosure footprint (worst case for slab rating); a single global 2.5× aisle factor; no tip/centre-of-gravity check.

Dials
  • chassis weightKg → rack weight & floor load · rack width/depth trades floor-load kg/m² against room area · anything that moves kW moves heat proportionally

Rack packing & fault-domain placement

analysis/rackSpace.ts · clusterPlacement.ts
Simulates

Chassis bin-packed into U slots (independent front/rear planes, first-fit), and — crucially — the gap between what a config promises and what placement delivers: three replicas in one rack share a PDU pair and a switch, so losing the rack loses all three.

The math

for each domain (rack/room/site/zone/region): surviving = total − largestDomain.members dataSurvives = copies≥2 AND domains≥2 AND surviving≥1 quorumSurvives = surviving ≥ floor(total/2)+1 verdict: single instance + multi-copy config → bottleneck ("replication isn't real") !dataSurvives → bottleneck · !quorumSurvives → warning

Assumes

Fault domains are hierarchical tags (no shared-spine/PSU modelling below rack); only the "largest domain fails" scenario is evaluated; a zone-less Azure VM is flagged because Azure may co-locate the copies. A bottleneck verdict rewrites the node's resilience — RTO becomes a restore, not a failover.

Dials
  • replicationFactor · actual machine rackId/room/site · Azure instance count/zone — spreading copies across domains is what turns a bottleneck healthy

Azure pricing — map, then price

analysis/cloudCost.ts · azurePricing.ts · server/azurePricingPlugin.ts
Simulates

Each on-prem tier → an Azure VM family/size, managed disks snapped to real SKU boundaries, ExpressRoute, and a container registry — costed against live Azure Retail Prices, falling back per-line to a dated snapshot. Every cost line records its basis (live vs snapshot) so an estimate is never passed off as current.

The math

compute = rate × riFactor × (730 × duty) × count // duty discounts PAYG only; a reservation bills 24×7 disk (fixed tier) = rate of smallest tier that holds sizeGb × count ER = portCharge(bandwidth, sku) + (Metered ? egressGb×0.025 : 0) ACR = dayRate×30×(1+geoReplicas) + overageGb×0.1 + egress×0.087

Assumes

Snapshot basis is East US / PAYG / Linux; RI discount is a flat multiplier (no savings plans / Hybrid Benefit); fixed-tier disks round up. The live proxy fetches VM and managed-disk rates only (6-hour cache) — ExpressRoute and ACR are always snapshot, even under "live pricing." The public Azure API needs no key.

Dials
  • vmSize · count linear · reservation (ri1y/ri3y) applies the discount, disables duty · dutyCycle discounts PAYG only · region chooses which live keys resolve
§4 Organization · value stream · services · rates · OKRs

The people side. Two constants make every figure comparable — WEEKS_PER_MONTH = 4.333 and fte = headcount × allocation% — and one principle governs meaning: wiring is truth (every edge's endpoints disambiguate it; config values are only fallbacks for un-wired elements).

The capacity ledger

analysis/orgMetrics.ts
Simulates

An org as a two-sided ledger of hours: roles supply them, meetings consume them. An org that never balances the two reports a headcount it doesn't actually have — the ceremonies are already spending it.

The math

capacity = fte × hoursPerWeek × 4.333 meetingHrs(role) = fte × Σ (durationHrs × perMonth) over wired ceremonies ceremonyPct = attributedMeetingHrs / capacity effectiveHeadcount = headcount × (1 − ceremonyPct) utilization = demandHrs / effectiveHrs // demand ÷ POST-ceremony capacity automation: combined = 1 − Π(1 − rᵢ) // tools stack multiplicatively, capped 95%

Assumes

A meeting wired to nobody still shows in the total but taxes no one (attributed vs unattributed — the gap is surfaced on purpose). Everyone in a role attends every wired ceremony at full FTE; effective capacity floors at 0; org-level demand isn't attributed to a specific role (that needs the flow model).

Dials
  • headcount / hoursPerWeek supply · meeting duration/perMonth + wiring attendees tax capacity · effortReductionPct frees FTE · org demand knobs drive utilization

Six Sigma — yield → sigma

analysis/swimlane.ts
Simulates

A cross-functional value stream's quality. The mathematical heart is converting a first-pass yield into a sigma level the same way industry does.

The math

flowEfficiency = workHrs / (workHrs + waitHrs) // value-add ÷ elapsed RTY = Π step.firstPassYield // pass EVERY step first time sigma = Φ⁻¹(yield) + 1.5 // Acklam inverse-normal + 1.5σ long-term shift DPMO = (1 − yield) × 1,000,000 // yield .99 → 3.83σ · .933 → 3.0σ · .5 → 1.5σ · .9999966 → 6.0σ

Assumes

Φ⁻¹ is Acklam's rational approximation (~1e-9 error, no lookup table). Steps are independent (RTY is a naive product); the +1.5σ Motorola drift is applied uniformly as a convention; sigma clamped 0–6; cycle time is a pure sum (no parallelism).

Dials
  • step firstPassYieldPct ↑ raises step & process sigma · more steps ↓ RTY · waitHrs ↑ kills flow efficiency · same-lane sequencing cuts cross-lane handoffs

Service roll-up — effort, not payroll

analysis/serviceRollup.ts · orgUtilization.ts
Simulates

A business service is charged the cost of the hours actually spent delivering it — a dev who spends 8 h/mo adds 8 h × their rate, not their whole salary — and per-person load is then summed across the whole portfolio to catch quiet over-commitment.

The math

effortCostMo = Σ step.workHrs × rate(owningRole) × runs // runs = each stream's OWN cadence peopleCost = hasProcess ? effortCostMo : org.payrollCost // headcount fallback only w/o a process utilization(person) = Σ(workHrs × runs across all services) / capacity

Assumes

Only workHrs costs money (wait is free queue time); one performing role per step (first owner wins); a step's cadence comes from its process register or the service default.

Dials
  • step workHrs · runsPerMonth · role loadedRateHr — and linking an architecture folds in its infra cost, p99 and bottlenecks (can flip service health)

Rates & staffing — skill × seniority, and reuse-vs-hire

catalog/skills.ts · analysis/gsaRates.ts · staffing.ts
Simulates

Price comes from the skill a role name resolves to, not the coarse node type; staffing a new service reuses people with headroom rather than cloning teams or silently overloading someone.

The math

rate = skillBaseRate × seniorityMult(name) // principal 1.45 · staff 1.35 · lead 1.25 · senior 1.15 · junior .8 // "Senior Data Engineer" = 175 × 1.15 ≈ 201/hr; a "Dog Groomer" resolves to no skill → its own identity staffing: match by SAME skill + headroom → assign; overloaded → expand (open reqs); no match → new hire GSA: applyGsaRates pins every role to its schedule ceiling; anything pushed above is flagged

Assumes

Rates are representative US fully-burdened figures; seniority is a flat multiplier; matching is lexical (curated aliases, no semantics); GSA ceilings are keyed by coarse nodeType; two different known skills never match (a "Lead Developer" won't be staffed by a generic "Developer").

Dials
  • per-node loadedRateHr is the master lever · role name (seniority words) applies the multiplier · Apply GSA rates repins + flags over-ceiling

Design-to-target OKRs

analysis/okr.ts
Simulates

A key result binds to a metric the model already computes, so its current value is derived from the design, not typed in and left to rot. It answers "does what we're proposing hit our targets" — deliberately no actuals or time-series.

The math

progress = clamp01( (current − baseline) / (target − baseline) ) // direction-agnostic // the sign of the span cancels the sign of the gap — the SAME formula solves "grow it" and "shrink it" status: ≥1 met · ≥0.7 on-track · ≥0.3 at-risk · else off-track · null unmeasured

Assumes

Linear progress baseline→target; only metrics the model genuinely computes are bindable; equal weighting of KRs; unmeasured KRs are excluded from the mean (not counted as zero); a single design snapshot, never a trend.

Dials
  • baseline / target set span & direction · the bound metric + scope choose the source · any design change that moves the metric re-scores it live
§5 Meet the experts

When you hit Tune with expert on a node, or ask the AI to design a rack, an Azure footprint, or a process, a named specialist answers. Each one is a persona — and their pedigree below is literally the system prompt the AI runs under. Change the bio, change how they think. They introduce themselves the same way: “I'm Larry, your data-centre engineer…”

A full pedigree, verbatim

The cards above are summaries — each specialist runs on a full brief: background → creed → the levers they know cold → the mistakes they refuse to repeat → hard rules → voice. That depth isn't decoration; it's what makes the advice specific instead of generic. Here's Larry exactly as the AI runs him when you ask it to design a rack — edit this and you change how he thinks:

You are Larry, laying out ONE rack. Twenty-two years in the white space — you came up pulling cable as a colo facilities tech, ran critical environments for a hyperscaler through three hardware generations, and have signed off on more methods-of-procedure than you can count. You've stood on the floor at 3 a.m. when a PDU let go, so you design for the failure, not the datasheet. Your creed: a rack that looks full on paper and dies when one feed drops is a rack you built wrong. Hard rules you never break: never load a circuit past 80% of its breaker; every redundant feed must carry the whole rack alone; heaviest gear low, airflow blanked, service clearance kept. You design elevations a technician could actually build, and you name the trade-off they didn't ask about.

Every one of the 22 has a brief like this. Want a sharper opinion or a different backstory from any of them? It's one paragraph away.

The Yeti says

Every number here is a model you can read, argue with, and tune — that's the whole point. A diagram asks you to trust it; a model shows its work.

Field Notes · ✦

Reference

Where your work lives

  • Workspaces → the workspaces/ folder, one JSON file each. Back them up or share them freely.
  • Settings & keys → .env, server-side only, never sent to the browser.
  • Team backend (optional) → point DATABASE_URL at Postgres and the switcher gains Push / Pull to sync a shared catalog across the team; without it, the local files just work.

Getting it running

  • Install Node 18+, then npm install && npm run build, then npm start → http://127.0.0.1:4173.
  • For live development with hot-reload: npm run dev → http://localhost:5173.

The laws on the wind

Conway's Law org ≈ system
Systems mirror the communication structure of the org that builds them. Design the org, not just the system.
Little's Law L = λW
Items in the system = arrival rate × time in the system. The foundation under every capacity and utilization number here.
Amdahl's Law S ≤ 1 / (1 − p)
Speedup is capped by the serial fraction. Even 5% serial work limits you to 20×, however many cores you add.
Universal Scalability X(N) → ceiling
Contention and crosstalk eventually cap — and can reverse — the gains from adding nodes. Why “where will it break first” matters.
The tail at scale p99 ≫ p50
Fan out to many services and the slowest one governs. At scale, tail latency — not the mean — is the experience.
Brooks's Law +devs → +time
Adding people to a late project makes it later. Every hire adds ~n communication paths.

That's the whole climb. Now go model something — and keep your layers pure.
